headline: A Home First: How England Is Ending Rough Sleeping
meta_description: England's new £442m rough sleeping programme builds on Housing First principles, giving homeless people permanent homes before tackling other problems.
summary_short: A proven housing model that prioritises stable accommodation over conditional treatment is now reshaping how England tackles rough sleeping.
body:
England is transforming its approach to homelessness by adopting a deceptively simple principle: give people a permanent home first, then help them rebuild their lives. The government's new £442m rough sleeping programme, announced in August, enshrines this philosophy into policy, expecting to provide more than 1,000 settled homes over three years alongside intensive support. The model, known as Housing First, reverses decades of conventional thinking that required homeless people to move through hostels and temporary accommodation, often while addressing addiction or mental illness, before earning access to permanent housing. Instead, it starts with housing itself—a settled home of their own—while support workers help access mental health care, addiction treatment, benefits advice, or reconnection with family. Crucially, keeping that home isn't conditional on accepting treatment or reaching milestones.

Michael's journey exemplifies why this matters. Homeless in Plymouth in 2022, he eventually reached London and slept on the pavement without even a sleeping bag before connecting with The Connection at St Martin-in-the-Fields. Through Solo Homes, the charity's Housing First programme, he secured permanent accommodation with rent covered by his benefits and mental health support funded by the charity. Gen, his assigned support worker, helped him settle in. After years of uncertainty, he now has stability and hasn't returned to the streets.

Evidence from government-funded pilots across Greater Manchester, Liverpool, and the West Midlands tells a compelling story. Among people followed for a year, 84% were living in long-term accommodation after six months, rising to 92% after 12 months. Loneliness fell from 35% to 16%, while GP registration jumped from 60% to 92%. Researchers found that stable housing reduced contact with the criminal justice system and antisocial behaviour, though employment remained low and some continued needing treatment for physical and mental health conditions. As support teams note, recovery is often slow and non-linear—but it becomes possible when someone finally stops worrying about where they'll sleep.
quick_facts: £442m government programme announced in August for rough sleeping
Over 1,000 settled homes to be provided within three years
92% of pilot participants housed after 12 months in programme
Loneliness fell from 35% to 16% among those housed
Housing First tested across Greater Manchester, Liverpool, West Midlands
